did_you_know.text: The word “nefesh” here means a person or individual, not only a “soul” in the modern sense. The word “bishgagah” emphasizes that the act was unintentional.

“The anointed priest” is the priest who was anointed with oil for his position—in other words, the high priest. The Torah emphasizes that even a spiritual leader can make a mistake and must take responsibility.
The blood is sprinkled seven times toward the curtain, showing how carefully the ritual is organized. The Hebrew verb “hizah” comes from the root נ־ז־ה, meaning to sprinkle or spatter drops.
The incense altar had “horns”—projections at its corners, not animal horns. Blood was placed on them, while the rest of the blood was poured at the base of the burnt-offering altar.

“Outside the camp” means outside the area where the Israelites camped around the Tabernacle. The chapter thus distinguishes between the sacred center of the camp and a clean place outside it where the bull was burned.
The chapter recognizes that an entire community can make an unintentional mistake without realizing it at once. Religious responsibility here is not only individual; it can also be communal.

The elders place their hands on the bull’s head, a gesture expressing the community’s identification with the offering. The elders represent the community, so every individual does not have to perform the act.
The word “nasi” is related to the root נש״א, meaning “to lift” or “to be elevated.” Here it refers to a leader or person of status, not necessarily a king.
The leader’s offering is slaughtered where the burnt offering is slaughtered, but its blood ritual is different. This shows that the place of slaughter alone does not determine an offering’s meaning.
In Biblical Hebrew, “am ha’aretz” is not a term for an uneducated person. Here it means an ordinary member of the people, rather than a leader or priest.
The phrase “a pleasing aroma” is a biblical way of describing an offering that is accepted and pleasing to God. It does not mean that God needs a physical smell as a human does.

The verse repeats the formula “the priest shall make atonement for him, and he shall be forgiven,” ending with a promise of forgiveness. The chapter therefore presents the offering not merely as a ritual, but also as a way to restore the relationship with God.
